unesco.title: Vimbuza healing dance
unesco.description:
Vimbuza is a healing dance popular among the Tumbuka people living in northern Malawi. It is an important manifestation of the ng’oma, a healing tradition found throughout Bantu-speaking Africa. Ng’oma, meaning “drums of affliction”, carries considerable historical depth and, despite various attempts over the years to suppress it, remains a fundamental part of indigenous healthcare systems.

Most patients are women who suffer from various forms of mental illness. They are treated for some weeks or months by renowned healers who run a temphiri, a village house where patients are accommodated. After being diagnosed, patients undergo a healing ritual. For this purpose, women and children of the village form a circle around the patient, who slowly enters into a trance, and sing songs to call helping spirits. The only men taking part are those who beat spirit-specific drum rhythms and, in some cases, a male healer. Singing and drumming combine to create a powerful experience, providing a space for patients to “dance their disease”. Its continually expanding repertoire of songs and complex drumming, and the virtuosity of the dancing are all part of the rich cultural heritage of the Tumbuka people. 

The Vimbuza healing ritual goes back to the mid-nineteenth century, when it developed as a means of overcoming traumatic experiences of oppression, and it further developed as a healing dance under British occupation, although it was forbidden by Christian missionaries. By becoming possessed by Vimbuza spirits, people could express these mental problems in a way that was accepted and understood by the surrounding society. For the Tumbuka,Vimbuza has artistic value and a therapeutic function that complements other forms of medical treatment. Vimbuza is still practised in rural areas where the Tumbuku live, but it continues to face oppression by Christian churches and modern medicine.

profile.name: Vimbuza healing dance
profile.tagline: Tumbuka trance healing ritual featuring complex drumming and spirit possession.
profile.insight: In mid-nineteenth-century northern Malawi, women dance their disease under a wool blanket while spirits speak their names from beneath.
profile.profile: A spirit-possession complex and healing dance practised by the Tumbuka people of northern Malawi, eastern Zambia, and southern Tanzania. Patients, predominantly women suffering from mental illness or physical imbalances, are treated over weeks or months by healers in a temphiri. Accompanied by women singing in a circle and men beating spirit-specific drums, the patient enters a trance to calm possessing spirits. UNESCO inscribed the tradition on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.
profile.profile_long: Vimbuza is a spirit-possession complex and healing dance practised chiefly by the Tumbuka people of northern Malawi, and among related communities in eastern Zambia and southern Tanzania. The term covers three related classes of possessing spirits—vimbuza, virombo, and vyanusi—the illnesses they are believed to cause, and the drumming, singing, and all-night dancing performed to identify and calm them. Vimbuza took its present form among the Ngoni-Tumbuka of the Mzimba and Rumphi districts during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, driven largely by the nineteenth-century Ngoni migrations remembered as the Mfecane. The convergence of Bemba, Bisa, Chewa, and Ngoni populations with the Tumbuka explains why each spirit class carries a distinct ethnic origin and speaks a different linguistic association. Vimbuza's emergence is also bound up with the disappearance of mwavi, the poison ordeal formerly used to identify sorcerers, which the colonial administration suppressed in the early twentieth century. Colonial authorities and the Free Church of Scotland's Livingstonia Mission, led by Robert Laws, viewed the dance with suspicion and sought to suppress it. A meeting at Elangeni in January 1920 laid the groundwork for a formal ban around 1924. Chiefs formed raiding parties known as kaphaso, wearing red caps, to confiscate and break drums. Despite these punitive measures, practitioners moved their ceremonies to remote areas at night, maintaining the ritual until after the Second World War. Attitudes shifted after Malawi and Zambia became independent in 1964, leading to state recognition of Vimbuza as valuable traditional culture. UNESCO proclaimed Vimbuza a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008. Illness among the Tumbuka is traditionally understood as an imbalance of hot and cold forces within the body. Treatment begins when a diviner-healer, or ng'anga, is consulted. In the first séance, known as kubunyisela, the patient sits covered head to foot with a blanket in a crowded hut while a small gourd, bells, and a drum are placed close by. An assistant of the same sex, called the musamu, addresses the concealed spirits, urging them to reveal their names. Once named, the musamu dresses the patient in standard costume: men wear feathered njukula headdresses, arm feathers, kabudula shorts, goatskin flaps called madumbo, and mangwanda iron ankle bells, carrying an mphomphwe hatchet. Women wear a duku headcloth, handkerchiefs, bracelets, goatskin skirts, and ankle bells. Vyanusi dancers carry a spear or walking stick and a fly-whisk. The dance proceeds as a dialogue between a soloist dancer and a responding chorus of women and children forming a circle, clapping and singing while men provide deep percussion on mubale-wood drums like the ng'oma yikulu and mphiningu. The therapeutic process culminates in the rite of chilopa, a blood sacrifice where the patient drinks fresh blood from a sacrificed bird or animal to transfer its life force and satisfy the possessing spirit. Alongside the sacred healing rituals, a profane entertainment form featuring satirical vigerembo songs and herbal stimulants emerged around the 1920s, offering a public voice for women navigating patrilineal marriage systems.

sections.origins_and_history: Vimbuza emerged among the Tumbuka of northern Malawi, eastern Zambia, and southern Tanzania during the nineteenth century, shaped by the Ngoni migrations known as the Mfecane and the convergence of Bemba, Bisa, Chewa, and Ngoni populations. It developed partly as a replacement for mwavi, the poison ordeal suppressed by colonial authorities. The Livingstonia Mission and colonial administrators instituted a formal ban around 1924 following a meeting at Elangeni in January 1920. Chiefs organized raiding parties with red caps, known as kaphaso, to break drums. Practitioners defied the ban by dancing at night in remote areas. Following independence in 1964, the newly independent governments reframed Vimbuza as traditional culture. UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The healing process involves structured stages. In kubunyisela, the patient sits concealed under a blanket in a hut while an assistant (musamu) coaxes the possessing spirits to state their names. Once named, the patient is dressed in specific ritual attire and ankle bells. The dance features a call-and-response dialogue between the possessed dancer and a surrounding circle of women and children who sing and clap while men drum. Sessions vary in length from a few minutes to twelve hours and culminate in the chilopa blood sacrifice, where the patient consumes fresh blood from a sacrificed animal to restore physical balance.
sections.music_and_instruments: Instrumental accompaniment is provided exclusively by drums carved from mubale wood, typically the large ng'oma yikulu and the smaller mphiningu, with Rumphi districts adding a third slower drum called mboza. Historically, Ngoni dancers used a basin-shaped dried cattle hide called an ingubhu or clashing war shields. Music is structured around a call-and-response dialogue between a dancer and a chorus, which ethnomusicologists identify as central to the therapeutic effect.
sections.costume_and_setting: Séances take place in a village house run by a healer, known as a temphiri. Costumes vary by gender: men wear feathered njukula headdresses, kabudula shorts, arm feathers, and goatskin flaps (madumbo, zamba, or nyisi), while women wear duku headcloths, handkerchiefs, bracelets, and goatskin skirts. Both wear mangwanda or mangenjeza iron ankle bells. Dancers carry symbolic items such as the mphomphwe hatchet, spears, walking sticks, or fly-whisks, alongside uniforms bearing white or red crosses revealed in dreams.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Vimbuza is performed when an individual is diagnosed with spirit possession causing mental or physical illness, understood as an imbalance of hot and cold forces. Predominantly involving women, the ritual functions as both medical treatment and a socially accepted release within patrilineal and virilocal marriage systems. A secondary, profane form featuring satirical songs (vigerembo or vigetyo) also developed to air social criticisms.
sections.notable_figures: Boston Soko (Tumbuka researcher who documented the tradition), Steven Friedson (ethnomusicologist who studied and danced Vimbuza), John M. Janzen (scholar of the ngoma tradition), Victor Turner (scholar of Ndembu drums of affliction), Robert Laws (Scottish missionary of Livingstonia Mission), Donald Fraser (Scottish missionary).
sections.regional_variants: Practised chiefly among the Tumbuka people of northern Malawi, as well as among related communities in eastern Zambia and southern Tanzania. Local variations exist between the Mzimba and Rumphi districts regarding drum composition, such as the inclusion of the mboza drum in Rumphi and historical variations in spirit classes (vimbuza proper, virombo, and vyanusi).
sections.lineage: Vimbuza belongs to the broader ngoma ('drums of affliction') therapeutic complex found across Bantu-speaking Africa, sharing historical and structural ties with similar possession and healing traditions in central and southern Africa.

profile.sacred_note: Vimbuza is a sacred healing ritual involving spirit possession and blood sacrifice; outsiders must approach with deep respect and avoid filming or disrupting healing ceremonies.

basic_steps: Sitting concealed under a blanket during kubunyisela

Call-and-response singing and clapping in a circle
teaching.rhythm: Spirit-specific drum rhythms timed with iron ankle bells (mangwanda or mangenjeza)
teaching.formation: Women and children form a circle around the patient and musamu
teaching.level_notes: Sacred ritual; instruction is restricted to traditional healing contexts and not standard dance classes.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Spirit-specific drum rhythms, call-and-response pattern between dancer and chorus
music_profile.vocal_style: Dialogue between a soloist dancer and a responding audience chorus
music_profile.sound_description: Two or three mubale-wood drums—the large ng'oma yikulu and smaller mphiningu—provide deep, far-carrying percussion audible for several kilometres. This is layered with ringing iron ankle bells and a powerful call-and-response vocal exchange between a solo possessed dancer and a surrounding chorus of singing women and children.

movement_profile.posture: Patient enters trance; dancers wear specific sacred garments and carry symbolic objects like hatchets, spears, or fly-whisks
movement_profile.footwork: Timed to drumming and iron ankle bells (mangwanda or mangenjeza)
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: carrying symbolic hatchet (mphomphwe) holding spear or walking stick holding fly-whisk
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Women and children form a circle around the patient
movement_profile.partnering: Assisted by a musamu (assistant of the same sex) and directed by a diviner-healer (ng'anga)
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Varies by spirit possession stage, sessions can last up to twelve hours

movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Do not interfere with sacred healing rituals, trances, or blood sacrifices; respect traditional restrictions.

episode_brief.title_hook: Dancing the Disease: The Trance Rituals of Vimbuza
episode_brief.logline: Explore the history, drumming, and healing rituals of the Tumbuka people's Vimbuza dance in northern Malawi.
beats: Introduction to the Tumbuka people and the ng'oma healing tradition in northern Malawi
Historical origins during the 19th-century Mfecane and survival through colonial bans
The kubunyisela diagnosis séance under a blanket
The vibrant circle of singing women and spirit-specific drumming
Costumes including goatskin skirts, ankle bells, and animal-derived symbols
The sacred chilopa blood sacrifice and its therapeutic role

drills: Review the roles of the ng'anga and musamu

lesson_ladder.goal: Analyze the therapeutic and possession dynamics
drills: Study possession classes: vimbuza, virombo, and vyanusi
Analyze ethnomusicological perspectives on trance and healing
Understand ethical boundaries around sacred healing rituals
